question: A transformation office asks Claude to score two hundred candidate use cases on effort and value from their one-paragraph descriptions, and plans to fund the top twenty exactly as ranked. What is the greatest concern?
options: A) The scored list will need reformatting before it can be presented to the executive funding committee.
B) Scoring two hundred use cases in one conversation may exceed what a single chat can comfortably hold.
C) A ranking drawn from short summaries can look authoritative while resting on assumptions nobody checked.
D) Some of the two hundred descriptions were written by staff who are quite unfamiliar with what Claude can do.
correct_answers: C) A ranking drawn from short summaries can look authoritative while resting on assumptions nobody checked.
explanations: Reformatting for a committee is routine presentation work. It changes nothing about the reliability of the ranking that the committee would be asked to approve.

Volume is a practical constraint that can be handled by working through the list in batches. It affects how the scoring is run, not whether a funding decision should be handed to the scores that come out of it.

Correct. A one-paragraph description does not contain the effort and value evidence the scores imply, so Claude must infer it. The numbers then carry an air of objectivity that a spreadsheet reinforces, and funding follows the ranking without anyone testing the assumptions underneath it.

Uneven familiarity with the tool affects how well individual submissions are phrased, and it is worth correcting, but it is a quality-of-input issue that sits well below the danger of treating an inferred ranking as a funding decision.
